question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=2 x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,2),$ then ${\int }_C\left(2 y\right)\,dx+\left(2 x\right)\,dy=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=2 x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(2 t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(4 t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(2 y\right)\,dx+\left(2 x\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(2 y\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(2 x\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(2 \left(2 t^{2}\right)\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(2 \left(t\right)\right)\cdot \left(4 t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}4 t^{2}+8 t^{2}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}12 t^{2}\,dt \\  &=\left[4 t^{3}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[4 \left(1\right)^{3}]-[4 \left(0\right)^{3}] \\  &=[4]-[0] \\  &=4\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y=2 \pi x^{2}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to point $B(1,2 \pi),$ then ${\int }_C\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x^{2}\right)\,dy=$ The composed integrand at the initial endpoint is interpreted by its one-sided continuous extension along $C.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y=2 \pi x^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\left(t\right)\,i+\left(2 \pi t^{2}\right)\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)&=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=\left(1\right)\,i+\left(4 \pi t\right)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_C\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\,dx+\left(x^{2}\right)\,dy &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+\left(x^{2}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\left(\cos{\left(\frac{y}{x^{2}} \right)}\right)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+\left(x^{2}\right)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}\left(\cos{\left(\frac{\left(2 \pi t^{2}\right)}{\left(t\right)^{2}} \right)}\right)\cdot \left(1\right)+\left(\left(t\right)^{2}\right)\cdot \left(4 \pi t\right)\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}1+4 \pi t^{3}\,dt \\  &={\int }_{0}^{1}4 \pi t^{3} + 1\,dt \\  &=\left[t+\pi t^{4}\right]_{0}^{1} \\  &=[\left(1\right)+\pi \left(1\right)^{4}]-[\left(0\right)+\pi \left(0\right)^{4}] \\  &=[1+\pi]-[0+0] \\  &=1 + \pi\end{aligned}
$$
